planting.note: Scatter seed over lean, rocky soil in early spring or fall and press in lightly, since seed needs light to germinate; established plants can also be increased from softwood cuttings taken in early summer.

directions: Plant in shallow, rocky, neutral to alkaline soil over limestone or dolomite in full sun, mimicking the open glades of the Ozark and Ouachita interior highlands where this woody-based subshrub naturally grows. It forms a low, twiggy mound with narrow blue-green leaves and produces bright yellow five-petaled flowers with prominent stamens through the summer months. Once established it needs no supplemental water or fertilizer and resents rich garden soil or competition from taller plants, so pair it with other glade specialists in thin, gritty, fast-draining ground. Light pruning after bloom keeps the woody base compact and encourages denser branching.

planting.note: Sow fine seed onto bare, gritty soil in fall so winter freeze-thaw cycles work it into the surface, or start in shallow trays over lean mineral mix before transplanting small plugs into rock crevices.

directions: Grow in thin, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun, the same exposed dolomite and limestone glade conditions this wiry little perennial occupies throughout the Ozark region. Its blackening dried stems (the source of the species name nigricans) carry narrow, almost thread-like leaves and clusters of tiny white to pale lavender tubular flowers over a long summer bloom period. It is extremely drought tolerant once rooted and spreads slowly by short rhizomes into a tight mat, making it useful as a durable small-scale groundcover between glade rocks. Avoid irrigation, mulch, or fertile soil, all of which encourage taller plants to shade it out.

planting.note: Direct sow cleaned seed onto shallow, rocky soil after the danger of hard frost has passed; this warm-season bunchgrass is slow to establish the first year and should not be mistaken for a failure, since most growth happens the second and third seasons.

directions: Plant in lean, rocky or shallow glade soil in full sun, the same dry prairie and dolomite glade ground where this fine-textured bunchgrass occurs across the Ozarks and southern Great Plains. The species name clandestinus refers to the flowering panicle, which stays mostly hidden within the uppermost leaf sheath rather than opening into an obvious plume like many relatives. Foliage is wiry and blue-green through summer, turning warm copper-tan in fall and holding its shape well into winter. It needs no irrigation or fertilizer once established and is best used in naturalistic glade restorations or dry native grass plantings rather than mown turf settings.

planting.note: Scatter seed over bare mineral soil, fine gravel, or thin rock chips in spring and press in without burying, since this tiny succulent germinates best with direct light contact and sharp drainage.

directions: Grow in exposed, shallow, nutrient-poor rocky soil in full sun, matching the thin mineral soil pockets on bare glade rock where this diminutive succulent naturally roots. Fleshy, cylindrical leaves rise from a small taproot, and small pink flowers open only in the afternoon for a few hours before closing, a trait shared with its fameflower relatives. It is one of the most drought-tolerant of the Ozark glade specialists and will rot quickly in ordinary garden soil or with any supplemental watering, so it belongs only in rock gardens, green roofs, or crevice plantings with extremely sharp drainage. Once established it self-sows readily in suitably lean, open ground.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall onto shallow rocky soil so winter cold stratifies it naturally, or divide established clumps in early spring; this glade goldenrod is far less aggressive than meadow-type goldenrods and will not overrun neighboring plants.

directions: Plant in thin, rocky, well-drained soil over limestone or dolomite in full sun, the specific glade habitat this goldenrod occupies within the Ozark Plateau and a few outlying Interior Highlands sites. Stems often arch or sprawl low across open rock rather than standing stiffly upright, carrying narrow leaves and ending in flat-topped clusters of small yellow flowers in late summer and fall. It is an important late-season nectar source for native bees and migrating butterflies on glades where little else is still blooming. Give it full sun and lean soil; richer, moister ground causes it to flop and lose the compact habit it shows on bare rock.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall directly onto lean rocky soil for natural cold stratification over winter, or cold-stratify seed in the refrigerator for 60-90 days before an early spring sowing.

directions: Plant in dry, rocky, well-drained glade or prairie soil in full sun, the exposed Ozark and Ouachita habitat where this blazing star is most at home. Densely hairy stems and leaves give the plant a soft gray-green cast and distinguish it from smoother-leaved blazing stars, while tight spikes of rose-purple flowers open from the top downward in late summer and draw abundant butterflies and native bees. It forms a deep taproot that makes it very drought tolerant once established but difficult to transplant after the first year, so site it carefully from seed or a young plug. Avoid heavy, poorly drained soil, which causes the crown to rot over winter.
